philosophy.objective: Build a repeatable research habit and improve decision quality; short-term benchmark outperformance is not the goal.
principles: The investor selects every holding and approves every trade.
Primary company and exchange evidence outranks news, market commentary and model opinion.
Price movement and technical signals are context; they cannot by themselves strengthen or break a business thesis.
Missing evidence must remain an explicit unknown and must never be filled with an assumption.
Doing nothing is a valid outcome. Activity is not evidence of good portfolio management.
Every material conclusion should name an observable condition that can confirm or falsify it.
Judge the research process separately from the portfolio return.

SKYGOLD.title: Cash-flow inflection
SKYGOLD.tldr: Sky Gold must turn rapid B2B jewellery growth into cash-generating growth: scale the advance-gold model, improve working capital and use the resulting cash plus the planned land sale to reduce debt. Exports and diamonds are upside, not requirements for the thesis.
SKYGOLD.coreThesis: Sky Gold can change from working-capital-hungry growth into self-sustaining compounding as the advance-gold model improves working capital and operating cash flow turns sustainably positive.
mustHappen: FY27 operating cash flow moves materially toward management’s stated positive ₹180–225 crore range.
The working-capital cycle improves as the advance-gold model scales across customers.
Debt and interest burden fall, including execution of the stated land-sale and debt-reduction plan.
supportingFactors: Scale, design breadth and relationships with large organised jewellery retailers support continued demand.
Exports and diamonds are optionality, not requirements for the core thesis.

thesisLegs.name: Core operation
thesisLegs.claim: A scaled B2B, design-led jewellery manufacturer serving organised retailers, with improving value-added mix and operating margins.

thesisLegs.name: Cash-flow transition
thesisLegs.claim: Advance gold and slower, higher-quality growth can turn reported profit into positive operating cash flow and lower debt.

thesisLegs.name: Exports and diamonds
thesisLegs.claim: New markets and product categories can add growth and margin, but the core thesis must work without them.

falsifiers: Operating cash flow remains materially negative without a credible temporary explanation.
Working-capital days deteriorate or customers resist the advance-gold model.
Debt or interest costs rise despite the promised cash-flow and asset-sale plan.
A major customer loss or promoter-related acquisition materially damages economics or minority-shareholder interests.

valuationFrame.interpretation: The forward valuation only becomes valid if revenue and margin guidance converts into cash. The committee must judge earnings growth alongside operating cash flow, working-capital days and debt reduction rather than rewarding reported PAT in isolation.

monitoringMetrics: Operating cash flow and free cash flow
Working-capital and receivable days
Advance-gold share of volumes
Net borrowings and interest cost
Land-sale completion and use of proceeds
Revenue, EBITDA margin and PAT margin against FY27 guidance
Revenue and concentration by major customer
Export and diamond contribution with their working-capital and margin profile
Related-party transactions and acquisition integration

evidenceSources.label: Company filings and results referenced by the approved deep dive

ANTHEM.title: Restocking recovery and CRDMO capacity ramp
ANTHEM.tldr: Anthem's FY26 slowdown must prove to be temporary destocking: CRDMO orders should recover, Unit III should contribute and molecules should keep progressing toward commercialisation. Unit IV and new modalities add upside, but the high valuation leaves little tolerance for weak utilisation or delayed growth.
ANTHEM.horizon: FY27–FY29, reviewed at each result and material capacity update
ANTHEM.coreThesis: The FY26 slowdown was substantially a temporary customer-destocking cycle; recovery, differentiated fermentation capabilities and new capacity should restore durable CRDMO growth as molecules progress toward commercialisation.
mustHappen: Subsequent results confirm that customer restocking produces a durable revenue recovery rather than a one-quarter rebound.
Unit III fermentation and other recently added capacity make a measurable contribution through FY27.
The Phase 3 pipeline progresses toward commercial production while Unit IV spending remains economically and financially controlled.
supportingFactors: Integrated discovery-to-commercial CRDMO capabilities and fermentation capacity form the claimed operating moat.
Near-zero leverage and strong historical returns on equity provide capacity-investment resilience.

thesisLegs.name: Existing CRDMO platform
thesisLegs.claim: Integrated chemistry and fermentation capabilities, commercial molecules and high margins establish a differentiated operating base.

thesisLegs.name: Restocking recovery
thesisLegs.claim: The FY26 slowdown was substantially cyclical and should unwind through renewed customer orders rather than require a new end-market thesis.

thesisLegs.name: Pipeline and new modalities
thesisLegs.claim: Phase 3 progression, GLP-1, ADC and other advanced modalities can deepen growth, but unattributed end-market forecasts are not Anthem revenue.

thesisLegs.name: Unit IV
thesisLegs.claim: The large expansion can extend the runway only if commissioning, utilisation and returns follow customer demand without damaging capital efficiency.

falsifiers: Revenue fails to recover after the stated end of destocking or management repeatedly resets the explanation.
Material molecule failures, withdrawals or customer losses undermine the commercial pipeline.
Capacity ramps without utilisation, cash returns or credible customer demand.
DavosPharma dependence, an adverse regulatory inspection or scientific-talent loss materially disrupts operations.
Earnings growth fails to support the high valuation over the thesis horizon.

valuationFrame.interpretation: The illustrative FY27 case is not company guidance. At this valuation the committee must demand evidence of durable restocking, commercial molecule progression and profitable capacity utilisation; sector enthusiasm or pipeline market size cannot substitute for attributable earnings.

monitoringMetrics: Quarterly CRDMO revenue growth and evidence of customer restocking
CRDMO and speciality-ingredients revenue and EBITDA mix
Commercial, Phase 3 and early-stage molecule counts and movements
Unit III utilisation and incremental revenue contribution
Unit IV capex, commissioning schedule and customer-backed utilisation
Top-customer and top-product concentration
DavosPharma-related revenue, terms and related-party disclosures
Regulatory inspection outcomes and scientific-employee attrition
Operating cash flow, return on capital and leverage through expansion

KMEW.title: FY27 bridge to a contracted marine-infrastructure platform
KMEW.tldr: KMEW's dredging business must bridge FY27 and replenish its order book while two green tugs are built for long-duration charters starting in FY28. The charter annuity is contracted but not operating, and shipbuilding remains valuable upside that must first be proven through on-time delivery and acceptable returns.
KMEW.horizon: FY27–FY29, reviewed at every result, material order win and vessel-delivery update
KMEW.coreThesis: Knowledge Marine is moving from a predominantly lumpy, tender-led dredging contractor toward an asset-owning marine-infrastructure platform combining dredging, shipbuilding and long-duration charter income. The re-rating is justified only if the existing dredging operation can fund and bridge FY27, the unusually strong Q1 FY27 economics prove repeatable enough, and vessels under construction convert into on-time, cash-generating charter assets from FY28 without excessive dilution, leverage or working-capital stress.
mustHappen: New dredging awards broadly replenish dredging revenue: quarterly book-to-bill should trend around or above 1, or the disclosed dredging order book must otherwise remain sufficient to support the FY27 bridge.

Subsequent results explain and substantially validate Q1 FY27's unusually high dredging segment margin; normalized operating economics must remain materially stronger than the roughly 30% downside case rather than depend on one exceptional contract.

The two contracted green tugs are constructed and commissioned in time for their October and November 2027 charter starts, converting capital work in progress into contracted revenue without material cost overruns.

The IWAI vessel programme, including the ten hybrid-electric passenger ferries due within ten months of the June 2026 award, reaches contractual milestones and establishes that the shipyard can deliver external commercial orders.
Receivables, debt and total project funding remain controlled while the company carries shipyard and vessel capex ahead of revenue generation.
supportingFactors: The March 2026 unexecuted order book was already weighted toward charter and hire, including two approximately fifteen-year green-tug contracts, improving potential revenue duration once the vessels begin service.
India's Green Tug Transition Programme creates phased, policy-backed replacement demand at major ports; it supports the opportunity set but does not guarantee KMEW further awards.

KMEW's approved ten-year tonnage-tax option can structurally lower tax on qualifying dredging and chartering income and release cash for fleet investment; shipbuilding and other non-qualifying income must still be taxed separately.
The first external commercial shipbuilding award covers ten hybrid-electric ferries for IWAI and includes five years of maintenance support, providing an observable proof point for the new vertical.
The planned shipyard near Vadhavan Port and domestic green-vessel policies create capacity and demand optionality, but neither is included as certain value until execution is demonstrated.
DCI is both an incumbent and a material customer or contracting counterparty, making the relationship partly complementary rather than purely competitive.

thesisLegs.name: Dredging bridge
thesisLegs.claim: The established dredging operation must carry FY27, but its order book requires continuing tender replenishment and Q1 margins require validation.

thesisLegs.name: Contracted charter annuity
thesisLegs.claim: Long-duration green-tug contracts can improve revenue quality after commissioning; they generate no operating proof while the vessels remain under construction.

thesisLegs.name: Shipbuilding platform
thesisLegs.claim: The IWAI programme and planned yard create material upside, but external delivery capability, margins and capital returns are not yet established.

falsifiers: The dredging order book falls below roughly ₹150 crore without credible replacement awards, or book-to-bill remains materially below 1 across successive reporting periods.
Operating margins revert toward roughly 30% and management cannot reconcile the Q1 FY27 margin spike to contract mix, execution or sustainable operating leverage.
Either green tug misses its contractual start materially, commissioning slips beyond Q3 FY28, or construction costs impair the economics of the fifteen-year charters.
The first external IWAI shipbuilding programme misses material delivery milestones or reveals that the yard cannot execute at acceptable margins and quality.
Receivable days deteriorate materially beyond the current roughly 109-day reference level, or capex produces sustained funding stress, excessive leverage or dilution.
Further material promoter selling, related-party concerns or weak disclosure reduce confidence that minority shareholders will participate in the platform's economics.
knownRisks: Green-tug construction, commissioning and cost-overrun risk
Capital intensity, negative free cash flow and funding risk

valuationFrame.interpretation: The valuation conclusion is dominated by which earnings base is sustainable. The committee must not annualise Q1 FY27 until the dredging margin and contract mix are validated, and must not value uncommissioned charter or shipyard capacity as if already earning.

monitoringMetrics: Quarterly dredging order wins, dredging revenue and book-to-bill
Dredging segment result margin and consolidated EBITDA margin
Remaining dredging, charter and shipbuilding order book by start and delivery date
Green-tug construction progress, cost to complete and commissioning dates
IWAI vessel milestones, deliveries and realised shipbuilding margin
Capital work in progress converted to productive fixed assets
Operating cash flow, free cash flow, net debt and receivable days
Effective tax rate split between qualifying marine income and non-qualifying activities
Promoter shareholding changes

KRISHNADEF.title: Bulb-bar moat funding three defence optionalities
KRISHNADEF.tldr: Krishna Defence's niche naval bulb-bar franchise must keep replenishing orders and converting growth into cash while WaveOptix electronics, VABO composites and the Jalkapi underwater programme are treated as staged optionality—not current earnings. The balance sheet is strong, but product concentration and a demanding valuation leave little room for weak execution.
KRISHNADEF.horizon: FY27–FY30, reviewed at every result, material order, qualification and project milestone
KRISHNADEF.coreThesis: Krishna Defence has built a scarce, qualified position in Indian naval shipbuilding components, led by bulb bars, and should benefit from the long-duration domestic defence and shipbuilding cycle. The investment works only if the concentrated core franchise keeps winning and executing profitable orders with sound cash conversion, while management commercialises its electronics, composite and underwater-vehicle programmes in measured stages without allowing early optionality, related-party exposure or simultaneous capex demands to overwhelm a still-small company.
mustHappen: The core defence and bulb-bar business replenishes its order book and sustains healthy revenue and EBITDA growth rather than relying on a short burst of tender execution.
EBITDA margin, working-capital days and operating cash conversion remain sound as scale and project complexity increase; PAT growth alone is not sufficient evidence.
VABO completes the remaining naval qualification process and converts approval into paid commercial orders with disclosed delivery economics.
WaveOptix produces verifiable operating progress and a growing share of associate profit without advances, guarantees or below-the-line accounting obscuring the core manufacturing result.
Jalkapi and the wider underwater-vehicle programme achieve disclosed technical, customer and commercial milestones while capex and funding remain controlled.
supportingFactors: Naval-grade bulb bars require specialised rolling, metallurgy and customer qualification, creating switching friction once a supplier is approved for hull-critical programmes.

Krishna Defence appears to be the only currently identified domestic qualified producer of DMR-249A naval bulb bars and supplies principal Indian naval shipyards, but neither an independent government register nor company disclosure establishes its exact market share by ships, tonnes or value.
Indian defence indigenisation and the multi-year naval shipbuilding pipeline create a durable opportunity set, although budget growth is not the same as attributable company revenue.
The April 2025 bulb-bar capacity expansion and Bureau Veritas certification extend the core opportunity into higher volumes and commercial shipbuilding.
Low reported borrowings and available liquidity provide some capacity to fund development, subject to working-capital and related-party discipline.

thesisLegs.name: Naval bulb bars and defence components
thesisLegs.claim: The qualified core franchise has scaled rapidly, but product-wise revenue and customer concentration are not formally disclosed and tender replenishment remains essential.

thesisLegs.name: WaveOptix defence electronics
thesisLegs.claim: The 40%-owned associate has developed RF-over-fibre capability; its revenue is not assumed to consolidate into Krishna Defence's operating revenue, and contribution must be judged through disclosed associate profit and cash economics.

thesisLegs.name: VABO composite doors and hatches
thesisLegs.claim: The 51%-owned venture could expand content per ship after naval approval, but successful tests and management timelines are not yet repeat commercial revenue.

thesisLegs.name: Jalkapi and underwater vehicles
thesisLegs.claim: The programme demonstrates technical ambition and strategic relevance, but no repeatable revenue model, contract value or delivery economics have yet been established.

falsifiers: Core order intake persistently trails core revenue, or the dated order book falls below a reasonable execution runway without replacement awards.
Core revenue or EBITDA growth slows materially while working-capital days, receivables or operating cash conversion deteriorate.
Bulb-bar or major-customer concentration remains high while the core franchise loses share, pricing power, qualification or naval programme demand.
VABO, WaveOptix or Jalkapi repeatedly miss disclosed milestones or consume material capital without customer-funded orders and measurable economic progress.
Material promoter selling, dilution, related-party transfers, guarantees or weak disclosure reduce confidence in minority-shareholder economics.
Earnings growth no longer supports the absolute valuation, producing simultaneous growth disappointment and multiple compression.

earningsCases.basis: Trailing earnings at the reference date

valuationFrame.interpretation: A lower multiple than selected listed defence peers does not make the shares cheap in absolute terms. The valuation requires sustained core earnings and cash growth; no premium is assigned to VABO, WaveOptix or Jalkapi until dated operating and commercial milestones are evidenced.

monitoringMetrics: Core defence revenue and EBITDA growth, not PAT alone
Dated order book, new orders, revenue execution and book-to-bill
Bulb-bar capacity utilisation, pricing and audited product mix
Revenue and order concentration by customer and shipbuilding programme
EBITDA margin, operating cash flow, receivable days and working-capital days
Net cash or debt, capex commitments and liquidity
VABO naval qualification, first paid order, deliveries and realised margin
WaveOptix revenue, profit contribution, cash flow, advances and guarantees
Jalkapi technical milestones, customer acceptance, contract value and capital required
Promoter holding, dilution, related-party transactions and contingent liabilities
Valuation versus normalised core earnings growth
openQuestions: What is the latest company-confirmed order book by product and execution date? The FY26 presentation indicates approximately ₹196 crore at 31 March 2026, while later third-party estimates require reconciliation.
What audited share of revenue, EBITDA and order book comes from bulb bars, the five largest customers and individual naval programmes?

Of the naval and commercial ships currently under construction in India, how many use Krishna Defence bulb bars, and what percentage of domestic bulb-bar demand does the company supply by tonnes and value? Management's approximately 4–6% figure refers to bulb-bar tonnage relative to a ship's deadweight, not Krishna Defence's share of Indian ships.
Was the approximately ₹45.6 crore specialised-steel order incremental to the March 2026 order book, and what margin and working-capital profile does it carry?
What qualification steps remain for VABO, and what customer commitment follows successful naval trials?
How are WaveOptix's associate contribution, ₹6 crore corporate guarantee and advances reflected in Krishna Defence's reported profit, cash exposure and contingent liabilities?
What are the contracted economics, delivery schedule and remaining capital requirement for Jalkapi and the Chennai facility?
How much of the historical promoter-holding change came from dilution, warrants or ESOPs rather than open-market selling?

evidenceSources.label: FY26 consolidated filing and related-party disclosures
FY25 filing confirming the WaveOptix stake increase

CREDITACC.title: Credit-cost normalisation plus Project Shakti diversification
CREDITACC.tldr: CreditAccess must grow through the microfinance recovery without recreating borrower stress, while Project Shakti expands retail finance toward 24–25% of AUM without sacrificing asset quality, NIM, ROA or ROE. A re-rating depends on diversification actually reducing cyclicality; one low-credit-cost quarter is not enough.
CREDITACC.horizon: FY27–FY29 for recovery and initial diversification proof; Project Shakti reviewed as a longer-duration strategy
CREDITACC.coreThesis: CreditAccess Grameen entered the post-FY25 microfinance recovery with greater scale, capital strength and operating resilience than many pure-play peers. The investment requires credit costs and profitability to normalise near management's FY27 ranges without renewed underwriting deterioration, while Project Shakti must progressively convert trusted microfinance customers into sound individual and secured borrowers. A durable re-rating depends on diversification reducing earnings cyclicality; one low-credit-cost quarter is recovery evidence, not proof that the structural microfinance risk has disappeared.
mustHappen: FY27 credit cost settles within or better than management's 3.0–4.0% guidance without relying on unusually low quarterly provisioning or aggressive write-offs.
AUM grows within the guided 20–25% range while collection efficiency, borrower indebtedness and early-delinquency indicators show that growth is not recreating the FY25 over-leverage cycle.
NIM, cost-to-income, ROA and ROE remain broadly consistent with management's FY27 ranges as credit cost normalises above Q1's unusually low level.

Retail finance grows from 20.6% of AUM toward management's 24–25% FY27 target, with separately disclosed asset quality, yields and vintage performance that demonstrate sound underwriting rather than simple balance-sheet reclassification.
Funding access, capital adequacy and liquidity remain resilient through the recovery and diversification investment.
supportingFactors: CreditAccess has the largest operating platform among Indian NBFC-MFIs and entered FY27 with capital adequacy materially above its regulatory requirement.
Industry guardrails on lender count, borrower indebtedness and bureau checks should improve new-vintage quality, but their durability across a full credit cycle remains unproven.
Project Shakti uses existing customer relationships to originate larger individual and secured products, potentially lowering acquisition cost and improving lifetime customer economics.
The FY27 recovery provides internal earnings capacity to fund diversification if asset quality remains controlled.

thesisLegs.name: Microfinance franchise
thesisLegs.claim: Scale, distribution, customer relationships and funding resilience are established, but unsecured group lending remains exposed to borrower leverage, agriculture, regulation and political intervention.

thesisLegs.name: Credit-cost recovery
thesisLegs.claim: Asset quality and earnings are recovering from FY25 stress; Q1 FY27's 0.72% credit cost is not assumed to be the sustainable run rate.

thesisLegs.name: Project Shakti
thesisLegs.claim: Retail finance mix has increased rapidly; confirmation requires continued book growth while maintaining acceptable credit cost, NIM, ROA, ROE and capital strength, and its secured and individual-loan vintages have not yet been proven through a downturn.

thesisLegs.name: Structural re-rating
thesisLegs.claim: A higher valuation multiple may follow demonstrably lower earnings volatility, but price stagnation or peer re-rating is not itself evidence of undervaluation.

falsifiers: Credit cost exceeds the FY27 guided range without a clearly temporary external cause, or new loan vintages show renewed deterioration despite industry guardrails.
AUM growth is achieved through higher borrower leverage, weaker collections, deteriorating PAR buckets or rising write-offs.

Retail finance fails to approach the 24–25% FY27 mix target, or Project Shakti's individual or secured products produce materially worse asset quality, adverse selection, weak unit economics or persistent margin dilution.
Capital adequacy, liquidity or lender confidence weakens materially, including covenant pressure or constrained wholesale funding access.
Regulatory pricing changes materially compress risk-adjusted margins without an offsetting improvement in funding cost, operating efficiency or credit loss.
Management obscures the economics or asset quality of the retail-finance transition through insufficient segment and vintage disclosure.
knownRisks: Valuation based on an unrepresentative earnings period

earningsCases.basis: Trailing twelve months after Q1 FY27

valuationFrame.interpretation: The apparent valuation depends materially on Q1 FY27's recovery and very low credit cost. The committee must normalise earnings toward management's full-year 3.0–4.0% credit-cost range and value Project Shakti only as its separate asset-quality and return record develops.

monitoringMetrics: Credit cost, provisions, write-offs and recoveries
GNPA, NNPA, PAR 0/30/60/90 and collection efficiency by loan vintage
AUM and disbursement growth versus active-borrower and average-ticket growth
Borrower lender-count and total-indebtedness distribution
NIM, cost of funds, cost-to-income, ROA and ROE
Retail-finance AUM growth and mix versus the 24–25% FY27 target
Retail, individual and secured product yields, NIM contribution, credit cost and product-level asset quality
Unnati and Unnati Lite cohort performance and repeat-customer conversion
Capital adequacy, debt-to-equity, liquidity and lender concentration
Geographic, agricultural and customer concentration
Final RBI pricing rules and quantified impact on yield and margin
openQuestions: How much of Q1 FY27's 0.72% credit cost reflects recoveries, provision releases, write-off timing or genuinely cleaner new vintages?
What are PAR, loss, yield and operating-cost metrics for Project Shakti products by origination vintage?
How much of retail finance is legally secured today, and what collateral, loan-to-value and recovery experience supports it?
Can management reconcile the ₹50,000 crore retail ambition and secured-mix target to the stated ten-year Project Shakti horizon and near-term capital plan?
What is the quantified effect of any final RBI pricing reform? The August 2026 proposal described in the investor note remains a forward item requiring primary-source confirmation.

evidenceSources.label: Q4 FY26 results and Project Shakti announcement
RBI regulatory framework for microfinance loans
